definitions.definition: A structural similarity between two different things, showing they work the same way even though they look different.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway lines — the structure is the same even though the map is smaller.

definitions.definition: The study of the brain and nervous system, how they work and affect behavior.
definitions.example: Neuroscience helps us understand why we feel pain or learn new skills.

definitions.definition: A condition where a person cannot stop using a substance or doing an activity, even when it causes harm.
definitions.example: Someone addicted to video games might skip homework and sleep to keep playing.

definitions.definition: When the body gets used to a drug or behavior, so you need more of it to get the same effect.
definitions.example: If you drink coffee every day, you might need two cups to feel awake instead of one.

definitions.definition: When the body becomes more sensitive to a substance over time, so even a small amount causes a big reaction.
definitions.example: After being stung by a bee, you might become sensitized and have a stronger allergic reaction next time.

definitions.definition: The wear and tear on the body from long-term stress, like damage from never fully recovering.
definitions.example: If you're stressed about tests for months, allostatic load can make you sick or exhausted.

definitions.definition: Unpleasant physical or mental symptoms when you stop using a substance you're addicted to.
definitions.example: When someone stops drinking coffee, they might get headaches and feel tired — that's withdrawal.

definitions.definition: When someone starts using a substance again after trying to quit.
definitions.example: A person trying to quit smoking might relapse after a stressful day and have a cigarette.

definitions.definition: When the brain's dopamine system, which controls pleasure and reward, gets out of balance.
definitions.example: In addiction, the brain releases too much dopamine from the drug, so normal things like food don't feel rewarding anymore.

definitions.definition: The brain's ability to change and rewire itself based on experience.
definitions.example: When you learn to play guitar, your brain creates new connections — that's neuroplasticity.

definitions.definition: The study of sin in Christian theology.
definitions.example: Hamartiology asks questions like 'What is sin?' and 'How does sin affect people?'

definitions.definition: The idea that sin can trap a person, making it very hard to stop sinning without help.
definitions.example: A person who lies a lot might feel they can't stop, like they're in bondage to lying.

definitions.definition: The process where sin slowly takes more control over a person over time.
definitions.example: Starting with a small lie, then bigger lies, until lying becomes a habit you can't break.

definitions.definition: A passage in the Bible where Paul describes struggling to do what's right even when he wants to.
definitions.example: It's like when you know you should study but end up watching TV instead, and feel frustrated.

definitions.definition: Being set free from something that holds you captive, like sin or addiction.
definitions.example: A prisoner being released from jail is a form of liberation.

definitions.definition: The process of becoming more holy or morally good over time, often with God's help.
definitions.example: A person trying to be more patient and kind is going through sanctification.

definitions.definition: The brain's way of adjusting to repeated drug use or behavior, often leading to tolerance.
definitions.example: If you take painkillers for a long time, your brain adapts so they don't work as well.

definitions.definition: A part of the brain that makes you feel good when you do things necessary for survival, like eating or socializing.
definitions.example: Eating chocolate feels good because your reward system releases dopamine.

definitions.definition: When a system adjusts to a new normal, often in a harmful way.
definitions.example: If you always eat very salty food, your taste buds recalibrate so normal food tastes bland.

definitions.definition: When you get less benefit from something the more you do it.
definitions.example: Studying for 10 hours might help a lot, but studying for 20 hours gives only a little extra benefit — that's diminishing returns.

definitions.definition: Harm that builds up over time from repeated stress or injury.
definitions.example: Running every day without rest can cause cumulative damage to your knees.

definitions.definition: When a system in the body is not working properly or is out of balance.
definitions.example: Dysregulation of sleep can make it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep.

definitions.definition: When something is taken over and used for a different purpose than intended.
definitions.example: A drug can hijack the brain's reward system, making you crave the drug instead of food.

definitions.definition: A person who can make choices between right and wrong and is responsible for them.
definitions.example: A human is a moral agent; a rock is not, because it can't choose.

definitions.definition: When you become less sensitive to something over time, so it bothers you less.
definitions.example: After watching many scary movies, you might become desensitized and not get scared anymore.

definitions.definition: When a person's heart or conscience becomes less sensitive to sin or moral wrongs.
definitions.example: A person who lies often might eventually feel no guilt — that's hardening.

definitions.definition: Feeling sorry for wrongdoing and deciding to change your behavior.
definitions.example: If you cheat on a test and then feel bad and promise not to do it again, that's repentance.

definitions.definition: Help or forgiveness that comes from outside yourself, especially from God.
definitions.example: A person who can't stop sinning might receive external grace through prayer or community support.

definitions.definition: How strongly a receptor in the brain responds to a chemical signal.
definitions.example: If you take a lot of caffeine, your receptors become less sensitive, so you need more coffee.

definitions.definition: A system that doesn't exchange anything (like energy or information) with the outside world.
definitions.example: A sealed jar with no air coming in or out is a closed system.

definitions.definition: When the body reduces the number or sensitivity of receptors in response to too much stimulation.
definitions.example: If you take a lot of painkillers, your brain downregulates pain receptors, so you need more medicine.

definitions.definition: The level of happiness or pleasure your brain considers normal.
definitions.example: If you win the lottery, your hedonic set point might rise, but then you get used to it and feel normal again.

definitions.definition: When the body increases the number or sensitivity of receptors.
definitions.example: In a dark room, your eyes upregulate light receptors to see better.

definitions.definition: How strongly your conscience reacts to right and wrong.
definitions.example: A person with high conscience responsiveness feels guilty after a small lie.

definitions.definition: The cumulative damage to a person's character from repeated sin without enough grace.
definitions.example: Lying over and over without asking for forgiveness builds up moral allostatic load, making it harder to be honest.

definitions.definition: When a person's moral character becomes twisted or damaged by sin.
definitions.example: A greedy person might become selfish and unable to share — that's character deformation.

definitions.definition: A condition where a person's spiritual life is unhealthy or damaged.
definitions.example: Feeling cut off from God or lacking purpose could be a sign of spiritual pathology.

definitions.definition: The body's ability to keep internal conditions stable, like temperature or blood sugar.
definitions.example: When you're hot, you sweat to cool down — that's homeostasis.

definitions.definition: A disturbance or change that disrupts a system's normal state.
definitions.example: A loud noise during a quiet exam is a perturbation.

definitions.definition: Related to disease or abnormal, harmful conditions.
definitions.example: A pathological liar lies even when there's no reason to.

definitions.definition: When repeated behavior strengthens brain connections, making the behavior automatic.
definitions.example: Practicing piano every day entrenches neural pathways, so you can play without thinking.

definitions.definition: A long-lasting strengthening of connections between brain cells, important for learning and memory.
definitions.example: When you memorize a phone number, long-term potentiation helps you remember it.

definitions.definition: The growth of branch-like parts of brain cells that receive signals, helping learning.
definitions.example: Learning a new language can cause dendritic growth in language areas of the brain.

definitions.definition: Not literally true, but used as a comparison to explain something.
definitions.example: Saying 'time is a thief' is metaphorical — time doesn't actually steal.

definitions.definition: Brain circuits that make you repeat a behavior automatically, even if you want to stop.
definitions.example: Checking your phone over and over can become a compulsive neural loop.

definitions.definition: The front part of the brain that controls decision-making, planning, and self-control.
definitions.example: When you decide to study instead of play games, your prefrontal cortex is working.

definitions.definition: A Latin phrase meaning 'end of itself' — a situation where the system that needs to fix itself is the same system that is broken.
definitions.example: A car with a broken engine can't fix itself because the engine is what needs fixing — that's Terminus Sui.

definitions.definition: The idea that external help (grace) is needed to reverse a downward spiral in a closed system.
definitions.example: A person stuck in addiction needs help from others (grace coupling) because they can't quit alone.

definitions.definition: A physics law saying that in a closed system, disorder (entropy) always increases over time.
definitions.example: A messy room gets messier on its own — that's the Second Law of Thermodynamics.

definitions.definition: When a person who was making moral progress falls back into old sinful habits.
definitions.example: A person who quit smoking for a month but then starts again is backsliding.

definitions.definition: The brain's process of removing unused connections to become more efficient.
definitions.example: If you stop playing piano, your brain prunes the connections for that skill.

definitions.definition: Happening gradually over time, step by step.
definitions.example: A progressive disease gets worse slowly over years.

definitions.definition: When tolerance to one substance makes you tolerant to another similar substance.
definitions.example: If you're addicted to alcohol, you might also need more sedatives to feel the same effect.

definitions.definition: Groups of sins that often occur together, like lying and stealing.
definitions.example: Gossip and slander often form a sin cluster.

definitions.definition: Affecting the whole system, not just one part.
definitions.example: A systemic disease affects the entire body, not just one organ.

definitions.definition: When a substance or behavior takes over the brain's dopamine system, making you crave it.
definitions.example: Drugs like cocaine hijack dopamine, making you want the drug more than food or friends.

definitions.definition: Worshiping or giving too much importance to something other than God.
definitions.example: Loving money more than God is a form of idolatry.

definitions.definition: The study of the church, its nature, and its role in Christian life.
definitions.example: Ecclesiology asks questions like 'What is the church supposed to do?'

definitions.definition: Helping each other grow stronger in faith and character.
definitions.example: Friends encouraging each other to be kind is mutual upbuilding.

definitions.definition: Essential for supporting a structure; if removed, the structure collapses.
definitions.example: A pillar in a building is load-bearing — without it, the roof falls.

definitions.definition: Chemical processes in the brain that affect mood, behavior, and thought.
definitions.example: Dopamine and serotonin are part of neurochemical mechanisms that affect happiness.

definitions.definition: The ability to make moral choices and be responsible for them.
definitions.example: A human has moral agency; a computer does not.

definitions.definition: The connection between a person and God.
definitions.example: Prayer is part of a divine relationship.

definitions.definition: Choices made by free will, not forced by anything.
definitions.example: Choosing what to eat for dinner is a volitional choice.

definitions.definition: Related to genes, the instructions passed from parents to children.
definitions.example: Eye color is genetic.

definitions.definition: Changes in how genes work that are not caused by changes in DNA itself, often from environment or behavior.
definitions.example: Stress can cause epigenetic changes that affect how your body handles anxiety.

definitions.definition: Able to be explained by simpler parts or causes.
definitions.example: A car is reducible to its engine, wheels, and other parts.

definitions.definition: When different things come together or become similar.
definitions.example: Two roads that meet at a point show convergence.

definitions.definition: Important as evidence for a claim or theory.
definitions.example: Finding a fossil is evidentially significant for evolution.

definitions.definition: Related to the properties of shapes and spaces that stay the same when stretched or bent.
definitions.example: A donut and a coffee cup are topologically similar because both have one hole.

definitions.definition: Related to measurement, like distance or quantity.
definitions.example: The metric system uses meters and liters.

definitions.definition: A measure of how fast a system changes over time.
definitions.example: A hot cup of coffee cools with a certain time constant — how long it takes to reach room temperature.

definitions.definition: A test to see if a mapping is specific by trying to replace one domain with another.
definitions.example: To test if addiction is like sin, try swapping addiction with learning — if it doesn't fit, the mapping is specific.
